**NVIDIA says US export controls on China could cut its revenue, hurt its competitive position, and disrupt its operations.** These points come from its FY2025 10-K. I only retrieved FY2025 passages, so this doesn't cover any later filing.

**Scope of the controls**
- Since 2022 the US government (USG) has imposed licensing requirements on exports to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. They cover A100 and H100 chips, systems built on them, and any future chip above set performance thresholds. [NVDA-2025-1A-0076]
- Licensing also applies to a wide array of products, including networking products, for certain end users and end uses in China. [NVDA-2025-1A-0076]
- NVIDIA says it has not received licenses to ship these restricted products to China. [NVDA-2025-1A-0079]
- The January 2025 "AI Diffusion" rule would add a worldwide licensing requirement for products such as the H100, H200, B200 and GB200, after a 120-day delayed compliance period, unless it is modified. [NVDA-2025-1A-0079]

**Licensing uncertainty**
- Licenses are slow to obtain, and NVIDIA has no assurance the USG will grant them or act on applications in time. [NVDA-2025-1A-0083]
- Approved licenses may carry burdensome conditions that NVIDIA or its customers decline to accept. [NVDA-2025-1A-0083]
- The USG reviews license requests in a closed process without clear standards. [NVDA-2025-1A-0083]

**Competitive harm**
- NVIDIA says the controls have already harmed its competitive position. They may harm it further if the controls widen in geography, customers or products, or if licenses are denied or delayed. [NVDA-2025-1A-0085]
- Rivals whose products are not restricted, or who can get licenses, may gain an advantage. [NVDA-2025-1A-0085]
- The licensing process makes pre-sale and post-sale support harder. It may also push Chinese customers toward alternatives from suppliers in China, Europe and Israel, or toward their own in-house solutions. [NVDA-2025-1A-0085]

**Risk of further tightening**
- The USG may change the rules at any time and bring more products under restrictions. NVIDIA warns it might then be unable to sell its inventory of those products. It might also be unable to develop replacement products that avoid the licensing requirements. That could effectively exclude it from all or part of the China market, and from other markets such as the Middle East and "Tier 2" countries. [NVDA-2025-1A-0086]
- Possible conditions include chip tracking and throttling mechanisms that could disable GPUs if they are used or located in unauthorized ways. [NVDA-2025-1A-0086]
- Controls could extend to more gaming GPUs, which could disrupt a significant part of NVIDIA's supply and distribution chain and hurt sales in the US and Europe. [NVDA-2025-1A-0087]
- Controls could also extend to networking products such as high-speed interconnects. Limits on data center GPU sales may also reduce demand for NVIDIA's networking products. [NVDA-2025-1A-0087]
- The USG may also restrict the import and sale of products that incorporate technology developed or made in China. [NVDA-2025-7-0009]

**Operational disruption**
- Much of NVIDIA's product is warehoused in and distributed from Hong Kong, so controls could disrupt its supply and distribution chain. [NVDA-2025-1A-0087]
- After the 2022 controls, NVIDIA moved some testing, validation, supply and distribution operations out of China and Hong Kong. It says any future moves could be costly and slow, and could hurt R&D, supply and revenue. [NVDA-2025-1A-0083]

**Mitigation and current position**
- NVIDIA has broadened its Data Center portfolio to include products that need no license. It has ramped China-specific products that don't need an export control license. [NVDA-2025-7-0007]
- Data Center revenue in China grew in FY2025. As a share of total Data Center revenue, it remains well below the levels seen before the October 2023 controls. [NVDA-2025-7-0007]

NVIDIA's FY2025 10-K describes US export controls on China as a major and growing risk. The main points are below.

**Restricted products and no licenses so far**

- Some networking products going to certain end users and end uses in China also need licenses. [NVDA-2025-1A-0076]

- The licensing process is time-consuming. NVIDIA has no assurance the USG will grant a license, or act on an application in a timely manner or at all. [NVDA-2025-1A-0083]
- An approved license may carry burdensome conditions that NVIDIA or its customers cannot or choose not to accept. The USG reviews requests in a closed process without clear standards. [NVDA-2025-1A-0083]

- NVIDIA says the USG may again change the rules and subject a wider range of products to restrictions. [NVDA-2025-1A-0086]
- If that happens, NVIDIA may be unable to sell its inventory of affected products. It may also be unable to develop replacement products that avoid the licensing requirements. That would effectively exclude it from all or part of the China market and other affected markets. [NVDA-2025-1A-0086]
- The January 2025 "AI Diffusion" rule would add a worldwide licensing requirement for the covered chips and systems. It would also create "Tier 2" countries, which include markets such as the Middle East. [NVDA-2025-1A-0079]

**Competitive and business harm**
- NVIDIA says its competitive position has already been harmed by the existing controls. It says that position may be harmed further over the long term if the controls change again. [NVDA-2025-7-0009]
- The licensing process makes pre-sale and post-sale technical support more cumbersome and less certain. It may also push Chinese customers toward alternatives, including suppliers based in China, Europe and Israel. [NVDA-2025-1A-0086]
- Data Center revenue in China grew in FY2025. As a share of total Data Center revenue, it remains well below levels from before the October 2023 controls. NVIDIA has ramped products designed for China that do not need a license. [NVDA-2025-7-0007]

**Operational and supply chain risk**
- After the 2022 controls, NVIDIA moved some testing, validation, and supply and distribution operations out of China and Hong Kong. Further moves could be costly and slow, and could hurt R&D, distribution and revenue. [NVDA-2025-1A-0083]
- Much of NVIDIA's product is warehoused in and distributed from Hong Kong, so controls could disrupt its supply chain. [NVDA-2025-1A-0087]
- Controls could expand to more gaming GPUs and to networking products such as high-speed interconnects. The USG could also require chip tracking or throttling mechanisms that disable or impair GPUs in some circumstances. [NVDA-2025-1A-0087]
- Limits on data center GPU sales may also reduce demand for NVIDIA's networking products used in servers with those GPUs. [NVDA-2025-1A-0087]

Apple says it depends heavily on outsourcing partners, mostly in Asia, for component manufacturing, final assembly and logistics. It presents this as a risk because it gives Apple less direct control.

- **Scale and location:** Apple depends on outsourcing partners for component and product manufacturing and for logistics. In FY2025 it says a "significant majority" of its manufacturing is done wholly or partly by partners located mainly in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, plus some sourcing in the U.S. [AAPL-2025-1A-0017] The FY2024 10-K used stronger wording: "substantially all" manufacturing. It also said a significant concentration sat with a small number of partners, often in single locations. [AAPL-2024-1A-0016]
- **Single-source reliance:** Apple relies on single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe for many components. Partners primarily in Asia handle final assembly of substantially all hardware products. [AAPL-2025-1A-0017] Apple adds that any partner failure can hurt its cost or supply of components or finished goods. [AAPL-2024-1A-0017]
- **Loss of control:** Apple says outsourcing can lower operating costs but reduces its direct control over production and distribution. It says this diminished control has at times hurt the cost, quality or quantity of products, and its flexibility to respond to changing conditions. [AAPL-2025-1A-0017]
- **Warranty and conduct:** Partner contracts may include reimbursement for product defect expenses. Apple still generally remains responsible to consumers for warranty service. It also says violations of its supplier code of conduct occur from time to time and can materially harm its business and reputation. [AAPL-2025-1A-0018]
- **Disruption risks:** Manufacturing, logistics and transit can be disrupted by several kinds of events:
  - natural and man-made disasters
  - IT failures
  - commercial disputes
  - labor, public health or political issues
  - trade disputes
  - geopolitical tensions or conflict [AAPL-2024-1A-0017]
- **Financial exposure:** Apple has invested in manufacturing equipment held at partners and made prepayments to suppliers under long-term supply agreements. If a partner or supplier has severe financial problems, supply could be disrupted. The recoverability of that equipment and those prepayments could also suffer. [AAPL-2024-1A-0018]
- **Switching costs:** Changing or adding to the supply chain takes considerable time and resources and brings regulatory and operational risks. [AAPL-2025-1A-0018]

Microsoft's FY2025 10-K names several kinds of AI risk. They are reputational and legal exposure, misuse of its AI services, heavy costs and execution risk, regulatory uncertainty, and competition.

**Flawed or harmful AI**
- Microsoft says AI algorithms or training methods may be flawed. Datasets may be biased, inaccurate, or insufficient.
- AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or harmful.
- Weak AI development or deployment practices, by Microsoft or others, could cause incidents. These could hurt acceptance of AI, harm people or society, or leave products not working as intended.
- Agentic AI systems that act autonomously may need human review of inputs and outputs. [MSFT-2025-1A-0034][MSFT-2025-1A-0035]

**Legal, regulatory and ethical exposure**
- Microsoft cites possible legal liability, regulatory action, and brand or reputational harm.
- Risks include intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims tied to AI training and outputs.
- New laws are emerging globally, including in the EU, and countries are diverging on how to handle AI. Microsoft will have to work across different regimes.
- Some AI scenarios raise ethical questions or affect human rights, privacy, employment, or society more broadly. [MSFT-2025-1A-0035]

**Misuse and security**
- Customers may use AI in unintended or inappropriate ways, or deploy it in high-risk scenarios.
- Some users may commit fraud or abuse through the services. Examples include unauthorized account access, payment fraud, and cyberattacks. Microsoft says its efforts to detect and control this may not be effective. [MSFT-2025-1A-0008][MSFT-2025-1A-0032]
- Products may have design or operational defects, or collect data in ways that don't meet customer or regulatory requirements. [MSFT-2025-1A-0032]

**Financial, execution and competitive risk**
- Microsoft is spending heavily on AI infrastructure, which reduces operating margins. If usage doesn't grow enough, revenue may not keep pace with those investments. [MSFT-2025-1A-0006][MSFT-2025-1A-0008]
- Investments in new technology are speculative, and AI products may not reach the margins Microsoft has seen historically. [MSFT-2025-1A-0009]
- AI is a highly competitive, fast-changing market with new entrants, including open-model and open-source competitors. [MSFT-2025-1A-0004][MSFT-2025-1A-0006]
- Microsoft also depends in part on AI developed by others, including its partner OpenAI. [MSFT-2025-1A-0034]

Microsoft's FY2024 and FY2025 10-Ks describe AI as a source of reputational, legal, competitive and financial risk. The main categories are below.

**Flawed or harmful AI output**
- AI algorithms or training methods may be flawed. Datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or biased or inaccurate. [MSFT-2025-1A-0034]

Apple's main foreign exchange exposure is that it is a net receiver of non-U.S.-dollar currencies. A stronger dollar hurts its reported net sales and gross margins. [AAPL-2025-7A-0001]

**Where the exposure comes from**
- The primary exposure is non-U.S.-dollar sales, cost of sales and operating expenses worldwide. [AAPL-2025-1A-0063]
- Gross margins on products sold abroad, and on products with components from foreign suppliers, have been hurt by exchange rate moves before. They could be again. [AAPL-2025-1A-0063]
- Exchange rates can also change the fair value of some assets and liabilities. [AAPL-2025-7A-0001]

**How currency moves hurt**
- **Weaker foreign currencies:** These reduce the dollar value of foreign sales and earnings. Apple generally responds by raising international prices, which could reduce demand. [AAPL-2024-1A-0067]
- **Competitive pricing:** Apple may choose not to raise prices. In that case the dollar value of its foreign gross margins falls. [AAPL-2024-1A-0068]
- **Stronger foreign currencies:** These generally help foreign sales and earnings. They could still push Apple to cut international prices, or cause losses on its currency derivatives, which limits the benefit. They can also raise the cost of components priced in those currencies. [AAPL-2024-1A-0068]

**How Apple manages it**
- Apple may use derivatives such as forwards and options, offset exposures, or adjust local-currency pricing. [AAPL-2025-7A-0001]
- Apple may choose not to hedge some exposures, citing accounting considerations or prohibitive cost. [AAPL-2025-7A-0001]
- Hedges may offset only a portion of the adverse effects, and only for the limited time they are in place. [AAPL-2025-1A-0065]

**Size of the derivative exposure**
- Apple's value-at-risk model estimates, with 95% confidence, a maximum one-day loss in fair value on its currency derivatives of $590M as of September 27, 2025. The figure was $538M a year earlier. [AAPL-2025-7A-0002]
- This model excludes the underlying exposures. Apple says changes in those exposures generally offset changes in the derivatives' fair values. [AAPL-2025-7A-0002]

**Apple's main foreign currency exposure is that it is a net receiver of non-U.S.-dollar currencies.** A stronger U.S. dollar lowers its net sales and gross margins when they are expressed in dollars [AAPL-2025-7A-0001]. The details below come from Apple's FY2025 10-K.

**Where the exposure comes from**
- Apple's primary exposure is to non-USD sales, cost of sales and operating expenses worldwide. Sales outside the U.S. are a majority of net sales [AAPL-2025-1A-0063][AAPL-2025-1A-0001].
- Gross margins on products sold abroad, and on products with foreign-sourced components, have been hurt by exchange rate moves in the past and could be again [AAPL-2025-1A-0064].
- Exchange rates can also change the fair value of some assets and liabilities [AAPL-2025-7A-0001].

**Effects of currency moves**
- **Weaker foreign currencies:** The dollar value of foreign sales and earnings falls. Apple generally raises international prices in response, which may reduce demand. If it chooses not to raise prices, dollar gross margins on foreign sales fall [AAPL-2025-1A-0064].
- **Stronger foreign currencies:** This is generally good for foreign sales and earnings. Apple may still cut international prices or take losses on its currency derivatives, which limits the benefit. Foreign-currency component costs may also rise, which hurts gross margins [AAPL-2025-1A-0064].

**How Apple manages it**
- It may use derivatives (forwards and options), offset exposures, or adjust local-currency pricing [AAPL-2025-7A-0001][AAPL-2025-1A-0065].
- It may choose not to hedge some exposures, for example because of accounting considerations or cost [AAPL-2025-7A-0001].
- Hedges may offset only part of the adverse effects, and only for the limited time they are in place [AAPL-2025-1A-0065].

**Sensitivity**
- Apple uses a value-at-risk (VAR) model on its currency derivatives. With 95% confidence, the maximum one-day loss in fair value was $590M at September 27, 2025, up from $538M at September 28, 2024.
- The VAR model leaves out the underlying exposures. Those exposures generally offset changes in the derivatives' fair values [AAPL-2025-7A-0002].

Apple is exposed to foreign exchange risk mainly because it sells in many currencies and receives more non-U.S. currency than it pays out. A stronger U.S. dollar hurts its results. The details below are from its FY2025 10-K.

**Sources of exposure**
- Apple is a net receiver of currencies other than the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar reduces net sales and gross margins when they are expressed in dollars. Exchange rates can also change the fair value of some assets and liabilities [AAPL-2025-7A-0001].
- The main exposure is non-USD sales, cost of sales and operating expenses worldwide. Gross margins on foreign sales, and on products with foreign-sourced components, have been hurt by currency moves in the past [AAPL-2025-1A-0063].
- When foreign currencies weaken, Apple generally raises international prices, which could reduce demand. It may choose not to raise prices for competitive reasons, and that would squeeze its dollar gross margins [AAPL-2025-1A-0064].
- When foreign currencies strengthen, sales and earnings generally benefit. Apple may then cut international prices or lose money on its derivatives, which limits the benefit. Components priced in those currencies also cost more, which hurts gross margins [AAPL-2025-1A-0064].

**Risk management**
- Apple may use derivatives such as forwards and options, offset exposures, or change local-currency pricing. It may decide not to hedge some exposures because of accounting considerations or prohibitive cost [AAPL-2025-7A-0001].
- Apple warns that hedges may offset only part of the adverse effects, and only for the limited time the hedges are in place [AAPL-2025-1A-0065].

**Quantified sensitivity**
- Apple uses a Monte Carlo value-at-risk model on its foreign currency derivatives. At 95% confidence, the maximum one-day loss in fair value was $590M at September 27, 2025, up from $538M at September 28, 2024.
- The model leaves out the underlying exposures, which generally offset changes in the derivatives' fair values [AAPL-2025-7A-0002].

**NVIDIA's manufacturing partners (FY2025 10-K)**

NVIDIA doesn't make its own chips. It relies on these partners:
- **Wafer foundries:** TSMC and Samsung make its semiconductor wafers. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- **Memory suppliers:** SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- **Packaging:** it uses CoWoS packaging technology. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- **Assembly, test and packaging of final products:** contract manufacturers Hon Hai (Foxconn), Wistron and Fabrinet. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- NVIDIA says its supply chain is mainly concentrated in the Asia-Pacific region. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]

**Supply chain risks NVIDIA flags**
- **Limited control.** NVIDIA doesn't assemble, test or package its products. It says this dependence reduces its control over quantity, quality, manufacturing yields and delivery schedules. [NVDA-2025-1A-0020]
- **Supply risks it lists.** These include no guaranteed supply of wafers, components or capacity, and suppliers pulling back on commitments. They also include higher wafer and component prices if it misjudges demand. [NVDA-2025-1A-0020]
- **Demand mismatch.** If NVIDIA underestimates demand and its foundries or contract manufacturers can't produce more, it may not meet customer orders. This could cost it revenue and market share. If it overestimates demand, it may not be able to cut its supply commitments in time. NVIDIA says mismatches have caused both shortages and excess inventory. [NVDA-2025-1A-0010]
- **Component bottlenecks.** Many products are part of complex data center buildouts. A shortage of any single component can therefore hit revenue broadly. [NVDA-2025-1A-0010]
- **Rising commitments and costs.** NVIDIA has paid premiums, made deposits and signed long-term supply and capacity agreements. These have raised product costs. It may still be unable to secure enough capacity. [NVDA-2025-1A-0010]
- **Complexity and inventory.** Adding suppliers and contract manufacturers makes production planning and logistics harder to manage. It also raises the risk of inventory provisions or impairments if commitments exceed demand. [NVDA-2025-1A-0014]
- **Geopolitical concentration.** Tensions involving Taiwan and China could have a material adverse impact. NVIDIA has critical suppliers, contract manufacturers and assembly partners there. [NVDA-2025-1A-0014]
- **Competition for capacity.** Competitors that own fabs may be able to take scarce foundry capacity and input materials when supply is tight. [NVDA-2025-1A-0008]
- **Quality and defects.** Relying on partners to make components reduces NVIDIA's direct control over production. NVIDIA generally stays responsible to customers for warranty defects. [NVDA-2025-1A-0023]

**NVIDIA depends on third parties for all manufacturing.** It uses foundries for wafers, memory vendors, and contract manufacturers for assembly and testing. In its risk factors, it flags supply that isn't guaranteed, concentration in a few suppliers and regions, and the difficulty of matching supply to demand. This comes from the FY2025 10-K.

**Manufacturing partners**
- **Wafer foundries:** TSMC and Samsung produce NVIDIA's semiconductor wafers. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- **Memory:** NVIDIA buys memory from SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- **Packaging technology:** It uses CoWoS packaging technology. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- **Assembly, test and packaging of final products:** Independent subcontractors and contract manufacturers do this work, including Hon Hai (Foxconn), Wistron and Fabrinet. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]
- **Regional concentration:** The supply chain is mainly in the Asia-Pacific region. [NVDA-2025-1-0029]

**Supply chain risks NVIDIA flags**
- **Less control:** NVIDIA does not assemble, test or package its products. Relying on suppliers reduces its control over quantity, quality, manufacturing yields and delivery schedules. [NVDA-2025-1A-0020]
- **Supply and pricing:** The filing lists these risks. [NVDA-2025-1A-0020][NVDA-2025-1A-0021]
  - Wafer, component and capacity supply is not guaranteed.
  - Suppliers may decommit.
  - Wafer and component prices may rise if NVIDIA misestimates demand or orders late.
  - Foundries or contract manufacturers may fail to secure raw materials or provide enough manufacturing or test capacity.
- **Process technology:** Foundries may fail to implement high-quality advanced process nodes and memory designs. [NVDA-2025-1A-0021]
- **Concentration:** There are few suppliers, and they are geographically concentrated. Losing a supplier could mean added expense and delays while a new foundry or subcontractor is qualified. [NVDA-2025-1A-0021]
- **Geopolitics:** Tensions involving Taiwan and China could hurt NVIDIA. Both are a significant part of its revenue, and critical suppliers, contract manufacturers and assembly partners are located there. [NVDA-2025-1A-0014]
- **Demand mismatch:** NVIDIA has paid premiums, made deposits and signed long-term supply and capacity commitments, and it may not be able to cut those commitments in time if demand falls. Past mismatches have caused both shortages and excess inventory, and the filing says they could happen again. [NVDA-2025-1A-0010] Inventory provisions or impairments are possible. [NVDA-2025-1A-0014]
- **Component dependencies:** Data center products need many components. A shortage of any one component can hurt sales of the finished product. [NVDA-2025-1A-0010]
- **Complexity:** Adding suppliers and prepaid capacity agreements makes it harder to manage production planning, execution and logistics across many suppliers. [NVDA-2025-1A-0014]
- **Competition for capacity:** Competitors with their own fabs may be able to take foundry capacity and scarce materials when supply is tight. [NVDA-2025-1A-0008]
